title: U.S. Space Force Awards $17 Billion in Rocket Launch Contracts to Seven Companies
excerpt: Combined with earlier awards, the NSSL Phase 3 program now exceeds $30 billion — the largest military launch procurement in history.
body:
• The U.S. Space Force on Friday awarded seven companies contracts under NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1, raising the program's ceiling by $11.4 billion to $17 billion.
  • SpaceX, Blue Origin, ULA, Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Impulse Space and Relativity Federal all received awards for national security launch services.
  • Combined with the earlier $13.7 billion Lane 2 awards, total NSSL Phase 3 contract value now exceeds $30 billion — the largest rocket launch procurement in U.S. military history.
  • SpaceX remains the only provider with an operational NSSL-certified rocket, as ULA's Vulcan and Blue Origin's New Glenn are both grounded.

The U.S. Space Force has expanded its flagship rocket launch program to over $30 billion in total contract value, awarding seven companies modified contracts under the National Security Space Launch Phase 3 Lane 1 program on Friday. The awards raised the Lane 1 contract ceiling by $11.4 billion, from $5.6 billion to $17 billion.

The seven recipients — SpaceX, Blue Origin, United Launch Alliance, Rocket Lab, Stoke Space Technologies, Impulse Space and Relativity Federal — will compete for individual launch task orders as missions are assigned. No funds were obligated at the time of the award, with the Space Systems Command at Los Angeles Air Force Base serving as the contracting activity.

A $30 Billion Launch Architecture

The expanded Lane 1 program complements the $13.7 billion in Lane 2 contracts awarded in April 2025, which cover the military's most demanding, risk-sensitive missions. Under those awards, SpaceX secured 28 missions worth up to $5.9 billion, ULA received 19 missions valued at up to $5.4 billion, and Blue Origin was allocated seven missions worth up to $2.4 billion.

Together, the two lanes now represent more than $30 billion in potential launch spending through the end of the decade, making it the most expansive military launch procurement ever assembled. The overall Phase 3 manifest has nearly doubled compared to Phase 2, with an anticipated 84 missions between fiscal years 2025 and 2029.

The Pentagon's fiscal 2027 budget request reinforces the trend, including roughly $5 billion for 31 national security launches — more than double the $2 billion enacted for fiscal 2026, according to SpaceNews.

SpaceX Dominates, But Competition Grows

Despite the broadening vendor base, SpaceX remains the only NSSL-certified provider with an operational launch vehicle. ULA's Vulcan Centaur rocket has been grounded since a solid-rocket booster anomaly during the USSF-87 launch on February 12. Blue Origin's New Glenn suffered an explosion during a static-fire test on May 28 that destroyed the rocket and damaged the company's only operational New Glenn launch site.

The newer entrants face their own timelines. Rocket Lab's medium-lift Neutron rocket, Stoke Space's Nova, Impulse Space's Helios and Relativity's Terran R are all expected to fly for the first time within the next year. Impulse Space's first Helios mission will carry government and commercial payloads, including the Space Force's Victus Surgo tactically responsive space mission.

Lane 1 vs. Lane 2: The Dual-Track Strategy

The Space Force's dual-lane approach splits missions by risk tolerance. Lane 1 covers "commercial-like" missions with lower security requirements, creating opportunities for emerging launch companies. Lane 2 reserves the most critical national security payloads — including direct insertion of heavy satellites into geosynchronous orbit and multi-manifest launches — for certified providers with proven track records.

In April, the Space Force also issued a sources-sought notice for 25 additional high-priority Lane 2 missions scheduled for fiscal years 2027 through 2029, comprising six launches in FY2027, nine in FY2028 and 10 in FY2029. That notice was directed primarily at existing Lane 2 providers, though the Space Force invited any firm that could demonstrate certification readiness to submit statements of capability.

Implications for the Space Workforce

SpaceX's Competitive Edge
›SpaceX is the only NSSL-certified provider with an operational rocket.
›ULA's Vulcan Centaur is grounded due to a booster anomaly.
›Blue Origin's New Glenn was damaged in a static-fire test.
›New entrants like Rocket Lab and Stoke Space plan first flights soon.

The expanded launch portfolio has direct implications for Indian-American professionals in the aerospace sector, who hold significant roles at SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab and their suppliers. The growing manifest — and the competition it fosters — points to sustained demand for engineering talent across propulsion, avionics and mission integration for years to come.

With the Pentagon now poised to more than double its annual launch spending, the scramble to build, certify and fly rockets on increasingly tight timelines will define the next chapter of the U.S. national security space program.
